title: Introduce backpressure-aware slice reservoir and gradual failover policy for perf canaries
author: Maya Chen
description:
Motivation: We see sporadic tail spikes and throughput collapses during canary traffic bursts that are correlated with upstream backpressure (queue growth and OOM retries). Existing canary detectors surface regressions but the rollout controller lacks a graceful mechanism to reduce canary exposure proportional to observed backpressure signals. This PR introduces a lightweight 'slice reservoir' that holds a fraction of traffic slices in reserve and a backpressure-aware scheduler that drains or releases slices based on measured queueing and host-level resource signals. The objective is to reduce noisy false-positive rollbacks and allow canaries to progress while avoiding catastrophic capacity collapse.

What this PR implements: 1) slice_reservoir component in the perf-canary service: an in-memory windowed allocator that partitions canary traffic into N slices and keeps a configurable reservoir count per canary. The reservoir can be tapped (release one slice) or sealed (hold) based on backpressure score. 2) backpressure score aggregation: a composite signal built from qlen growth rate, retry rate, and host CPU-steal. Score -> [0,1]. 3) scheduler policy: maps score to release/hold cadence and integrates with the existing rollout controller so partial traffic ramps are smoothed rather than abruptly cut. 4) gradual_failover policy: if score exceeds severe thresholds the policy triggers a staged failover with staged-cork -> probe-only -> full-fallback instead of instant rollback. 5) metrics + tracing: added metrics (slice_reservoir.released, .held, backpressure.score, failover.stage) and spans for slice operations to help debugging. 6) integration tests and a stress harness that simulates queue pressure to assert staged behavior.

Why this is different: Instead of treating backpressure as a binary signal, the slice reservoir lets the system modulate exposure in fine-grained steps and provides a documented staged failover path that preserves availability for non-impacted tenants. This reduces oscillation between rollout/rollback and increases the chance of detecting soft regressions that self-stabilize once KV cache warms.

Compatibility and config: The new subsystem is disabled by default. Operator flags: --canary-slice-count (default 8), --slice-reservoir-size (default 2), --backpressure-weighting (qlen:0.5,retries:0.3,cpu:0.2), --enable-gradual-failover (false). We add a Console toggle for early canary cohorts.

Testing and results: We ran the stress harness across 3 clusters (dev/staging/canary) with synthetic load that induces queue growth. In experiments where current system fails (~30% throughput loss within 45s), the slice reservoir path reduced catastrophic loss to under 6% while still surfacing a progressive latency signal. Tail p99 decreased by up to 18% under backpressure compared to the uncontrolled rollout.

Rollout plan: Start feature-flagged in canary environment for 48h, enable for 10% of internal traffic, collect metrics for 7 days, then opt-in to public canaries. Linear ENG-4219 tracks the rollout and dashboard changes.

Notes: This touches perf-canary scheduling logic and a thin surface area of rollout controller; no model-serving runtime kernel changes. No breaking API changes.
